forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough has £10.6m of in-principle exceptional financial support across 2025/26 and 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council was provided with in-principle capitalisation support of £10.6m across 2025/26 and 2026/27, according to an update to its Audit Committee on the council's Exceptional Financial Support action plan. The support is split £5m in 2025/26 and £5.6m in 2026/27. The council formally requested it from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government in December 2025.

Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The paper says a review by the accountancy body CIPFA assessed financial management, financial sustainability and risk, service reform and transformation, and governance, culture and leadership. It "concluded that the Council had credible plans to improve financial sustainability and reduce its reliance on Exceptional Financial Support." The paper describes this as a conclusion about the plans, not a statement that they have been delivered.

The action plan appendix rates one recommendation, number 8 on reserves, as High, scoring it 9. It states: "Reserves remain low and mean that the council does not have the financial resilience to deal with unexpected financial shocks, remaining reliant on Exceptional Financial Support." The action listed is to set a risk-based minimum reserves level as a percentage of net revenue expenditure, and to monitor replenishment against the medium-term financial strategy.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough has government approval to capitalise £9.7m of costs; SEND report raises further support
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council has agreed with government to capitalise £9.7m of extraordinary day-to-day spending pressures under exceptional financial support, permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The medium-term financial strategy before Cabinet on 27 October 2026 says the sum is made up of £4.0m for 2025/26 and £5.7m for 2026/27.

The approval followed a review by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA), published on 18 August. The strategy says the review found significant improvements in financial management and governance, and that challenges remain, including rebuilding reserves and pressures in children's social care.

A separate Cabinet report on reform of support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) says the council would need to consider exceptional financial support again. It links this to the council's low reserve balances and to the possibility that the Department for Education funds only 90% of future deficits. The report says "the Council would need to consider Exceptional Financial Support to fund this", meaning the remaining 10%.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough forecasts £7.9m overspend on £258m budget, £7.7m of it in children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to spend £7.9m more than planned in 2026/27 on its day-to-day running costs (revenue spending: staff, services and contracts). That is 3.1% over a net budget of £258m, according to a first-quarter report to its cabinet on 1 October. Children and Young People accounts for £7.7m of the total.

The largest single line is placements for children in care, forecast to overspend by £5.2m. The budget assumed 429 children in care and 41 residential placements. The number of children in care was 444 in June, and residential placements stood at 47 in August. The average price of the last ten residential placements is £9,000 a week against £6,500 budgeted, and nine children are in placements costing more than £10,000 a week. Residential care makes up £3.2m of the £5.2m placement overspend.

If the overspend continues to the year end, the council will have to draw on its general fund reserves, the money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected. The report forecasts the balance falling from £10.5m at the start of the year to £6.7m by 31 March 2027, a 36% reduction. Total usable reserves, money the council can actually spend, are £23.7m, excluding the deficit on schools funding. Of that, £6.8m, or 29%, is ringfenced for specific purposes.

findings.headline: Council has applied to MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support, alongside a Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Policy approved in February 2026
findings.detail: The paper says these measures have been put in place to protect and rebuild reserves. It also says a full review of reserve commitments has released or reprofiled £1.6m. Reserves are forecast to fall over the medium term, and the paper says rebuilding remains a longer-term priority.
findings.matters: An application for Exceptional Financial Support is a formal request to central government for support, and the flexible capital receipts policy and £1.6m of released reserves are tools other councils in similar positions may be considering.
findings.figures: £1.6m of reserve commitments released or reprofiled; £24.5m total usable reserves, ring-fenced reserves and General Fund balance at 31 March 2027 (excluding DSG)
findings.quote: the application to MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast at £104m against a £148m budget, with c£51m of borrowing likely required
findings.detail: The paper says only £34m (23%) of the programme has been spent or committed at the halfway point, and a review has identified further slippage. Of the £104m forecast, £53m is funded by grants or third-party contributions and £51m by corporate resources. The Place & Economy Renewable Energy Projects line shows a £13.4m projected underspend against a £13.6m budget.
findings.matters: A forecast that depends on about £51m of borrowing or capital receipts, with a large share of the budget slipping, is directly relevant to borrowing requirements and to treasury planning at other councils.
findings.figures: £104m forecast spend; £148m programme (70%); £34m spent or committed (23%); £51m corporate resources (borrowing or capital receipts); £53m grants or third-party funding; £43.7m projected variance
findings.quote: This expenditure is likely to require c£51m of borrowing

findings.headline: Clare Lodge secure unit occupancy at 7 against an assumed 8 for the rest of the year, with reduced income of £4.7m offset by reserve to £3.9m
findings.detail: The business plan assumed average occupancy of 9.8 for the year. Two Ofsted admission restrictions held occupancy at 4 until the end of June. The paper says the restrictions were lifted in early May and occupancy is now 7, rising from 5 in July and 6 in September. The forecast assumes occupancy of 8 to year end, and says a further deficit will occur if this is not achieved.
findings.matters: The unit's occupancy recovery and the reserve offset are specific mechanisms other councils running secure units will recognise, and the paper states the forecast depends on a specific occupancy level being reached.
findings.figures: £4.7m reduced income reduced by reserve to £3.9m; occupancy 4 to 7 (current); 9.8 budgeted average occupancy; 8 assumed to year end
findings.quote: £4.7m reduced income at Clare Lodge, reduced by reserve off-set to £3.9m.

findings.headline: Savings programme at quarter 2: 34% realised, 33% green, 22% amber and 11% red
findings.detail: The paper reports the RAG status of the savings programme and says 33% of savings are rated red or amber. The largest risks are Culture and Leisure savings (£1.3m ongoing pressure after a Mutual Ventures cost baseline assessment), Regulatory Services Housing Standards (£1.1m of a £1.9m target at risk), and Children's Residential Homes (£0.3m, not yet started). The paper says red-rated savings are reported as pressures in the forecast.
findings.matters: Savings slippage at this scale, and the statement that red-rated savings are already in the forecast, shows how a council is turning delivery risk into reported pressure, which peers and lenders can compare against their own savings tracking.
findings.figures: 34% blue (realised); 33% green; 22% amber; 11% red; £1.3m Culture and Leisure ongoing pressure; £1.1m of £1.9m Housing Standards target at risk; £0.3m Children's Residential Homes

findings.headline: General Fund balance forecast to fall to £7m at 31 March 2027, below the £12.1m CIPFA recommendation
findings.detail: The paper says CIPFA recommends holding 5% of the net revenue budget in the General Fund, which would be £12.1m on the 2026/27 budget. The planned reserve rebuilding contributions have been removed from the MTFS because they are needed to bridge budget gaps. The paper says the General Fund projection includes a contribution linked to the Exceptional Financial Support request.
findings.matters: A General Fund balance well below the CIPFA benchmark, with planned rebuilding removed, is a direct signal of reduced financial resilience for finance directors and lenders assessing the council.
findings.figures: £7m forecast General Fund at 31 March 2027; £12.1m CIPFA-recommended 5% level; £257m net revenue budget; £9.7m in-year overspend
findings.quote: the council should hold £12.1m, but as set out in section 7 the council expects to have £7m remaining at the end of the year
